newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Opinion polls on trial in British election.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Opinion polls on trial in British election.

text.p: Britain appears to want a change of government. The opinion pollsters say they will get it.
But does anyone believe them?
As the country prepares for a May 1 election, the polls are unanimous that the Conservatives, in power since 1979, will be replaced by a Labour government.

Since the beginning of March, NOP, Gallup, ICM and Harris have put Labour's lead at between 21 and 28 percentage points, a huge lead. No government has entered a British election campaign as far behind and won.
But behind these confident predictions, the polling organisations are nervous, still picking at the scars left by their 1992 debacle.

What was forecast as a narrow Labour victory at the last election turned into a Conservative celebration as Prime Minister John Major rode back into office on the back of an overall majority of 21 -- 64 seats more than Labour.
Nick Moon, head of Social and Political Research at NOP, which runs surveys for Reuters and the Sunday Times, said pollsters had tightened their approach in the past five years.
"The polls' record was seriously tainted by 1992 but before that it was extremely good. 1992 was a one-off," he said.

"From a public relations point of view, the key thing that went wrong in 1992 was that they called it wrong," said Sheffield University politics professor Paul Whiteley. "This time it's pretty clear that Labour are going to win the election."
UPDATING DATA TO GET IT RIGHT THIS TIME

A post-mortem by Britain's Market Research Society into how the polls misread the Conservatives' popularity prompted pollsters to adapt their methods. This time they are determined to prove they can get it right down to a few percentage points.

Voting trend expert Peter Kellner saw seven areas of potential bias in 1992 which he said contributed to a four percentage point overestimate of Labour's share of the vote and a four point underestimate for the Conservatives.

Kellner says the mistakes included faulty samples, assumptions that people who were available for interviews had the same opinions as those who were not or who refused to take part, late changes of mind and the reluctance of Conservative voters to declare their allegiance, the so-called shame factor.

Companies have updated the demographic data to improve their sampling accuracy. They now typically check whether respondents own their cars or homes as well as matching their samples to the overall population by age and sex.

But even with these changes in method, are the results right? Political analysts who pore over the polls say yes, up to a point. The numbers that fail to make it to the front pages of newspapers hold important lessons for the pollsters, they say.

For instance, much depends on how pollsters treat an inconclusive answer to the question: "Who would you vote for if there were an election tomorrow?". Some say they do not know, others refuse to say anything and others say they will not vote.
The "don't knows" include some of the most important targets for the political parties themselves -- the quarter of all voters who will make up their minds in the last weeks of campaigning.
Most pollsters get round this imprecision by adjusting the responses for how the same people said they voted in 1992. Many Britons changed their minds in the last hours of the 1992 campaign.
"SILENT" VOTERS CAUSE DOUBTS

Nick Sparrow of ICM, which polls for the Guardian newspaper, elaborates a "spiral of silence" theory to prove that in the present climate many previous Conservative voters refuse to admit how they voted before.
More people remember voting Labour last time than is borne out by the real election outcome, he says.
But "there is no proof at all that one sort of adjustment gets it right or wrong," Sparrow says.
While few worry that 1997 will go down with 1992 and 1970 as a year the polls got the wrong winner, their consistent signals of an impending Labour landslide still cause doubts.
One organisation's decision to change to telephone polling from face-to-face caused a sharp fall in Labour's lead, raising eyebrows among politicians at just how accurate polling can be.

"Are we 28 points ahead...Are we going to win by a landslide? I doubt it," Labour's election campaign planner, Peter Mandelson, said on Tuesday. The Conservatives brush off polls with the jibe "look what happened in 1992".
Politicians, both Labour and Conservatives, believe the race will be much closer on polling day than the polls show.

"We don't know if history repeats itself at this election, but I'm looking at these statistics to say 'The Tories aren't down and out yet,'" said Michael Thrasher, political analyst at Plymouth University, of the results of an NOP poll this week.
One hope for the government is that voters, particularly disenchanted Conservatives, will change their vote at the last minute to stop Labour having too large a parliamentary majority.
As MORI chairman Robert Worcester says, when it grasps the message of the Labour lead in the polls: "The British public is going to react like a mongoose to a cobra".
